question: When you drag your social media feed down with your thumb and wait to see whether anything new pops up, critics say you are basically playing which casino device?
source_excerpt: Harris told the US Senate Commerce Committee that the downward pull works like a slot machine lever, keeping people pulling even when nothing was there.

extra.why_interesting: Players do this gesture dozens of times a day without thinking about it. The answer recasts an everyday swipe as a gambling mechanism, and most players can reason their way there from the 'pull and wait' description.
extra.verification_notes: Pull-to-refresh is widely likened to a slot machine lever by critics such as Tristan Harris; no newer development contradicts this (https://uxdesign.cc/your-personal-slot-machine-how-design-can-hack-your-brain-6a288c379ac7).

explanation: It is the same trick as a one-armed bandit: you pull, wait, and sometimes win, and that unpredictable reward keeps you coming back. Even the gesture's inventor later admitted that pull-to-refresh is addictive.

question: You feel your phone buzz in your pocket, pull it out, and there is nothing there at all. This ghostly sensation has a name. What is it called?
source_excerpt: Phantom vibration syndrome is the false perception that your mobile phone is vibrating or ringing when it isn't.

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone has felt a buzz, checked, and found nothing, but few realise the experience has an established name or how common it is. The 'ghostly' framing gives a fair foothold toward the key word 'phantom' without giving away the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Phantom vibration syndrome is the standard name for perceiving a phone vibration that isn't there; alternate names like ringxiety are secondary (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_vibration_syndrome).

explanation: In one study nearly nine out of ten students said it happens to them. A brain primed for notifications starts reading any small twitch of clothing or muscle as a buzz.
